endorsements.quote: Lastly, our approach keeps the allocation of decision responsibility with humans and preserves their autonomy, attesting to its strong sociotechnical foundations.

These observations reinforce the relevance of ante-hoc interpretable artificial intelligence whose inherent soundness and human intelligibility are guaranteed by means of constraining the underlying model form, e.g., to account for application-specific requirements, making it suitable for high stakes domains like healthcare 18 , 104 .

unlisted_practices: Design AI decision-support tools to complement clinicians' cognitive and epistemic functions rather than deliver ready-made conclusions that replace their judgement.
Select the automation paradigm (autonomy, assistance, or augmentation) independently for each cognitive activity based on the task's automation readiness level.
Design clinical AI to account for temporality and patient trajectories instead of independent point-in-time predictions.
Incorporate cognitive forcing, base-rate updating, and immediate feedback techniques into AI decision support to reduce cognitive biases.
Build AI tools that let clinicians run mental simulations of alternative patient trajectories conditioned on missing or unknown information.
Develop clinical AI with interdisciplinary teams that integrate the tool into existing workflows, organisational structures, and institutional constraints.
Test medical AI prospectively in real-life clinical settings to overcome the translational barrier.
Ensure clinical AI models use only information available at the time of real-time deployment, avoiding future information leakage.

screen.reason: The paper is a perspective/conceptual framework proposing a novel sociotechnical conceptualisation of AI support tools to support clinical reasoning and bridge the translational gap.
